segments.text: By the early 20th century, several experiments could not be explained by classical (Newtonian and Maxwellian) physics: the photoelectric effect, atomic spectra, and the stability of atoms themselves. Quantum mechanics was developed to resolve these failures, and it replaces classical certainty with a probabilistic description of nature at small scales.

blocks.text: 1. Wave–particle duality and the de Broglie hypothesis

segments.text: Light, previously understood as a wave (Chapter III), was shown by the photoelectric effect (below) to also behave as discrete particles (photons). De Broglie extended this duality in the opposite direction, proposing that matter itself has an associated wavelength, λ = h/p (h is Planck’s constant, p is momentum). This was confirmed experimentally by electron diffraction, showing that electrons — normally thought of as particles — produce interference patterns just like waves.
Wave–particle duality
means that quantum objects are neither purely particles nor purely waves; which behaviour is observed depends on the type of measurement performed.
In quantum mechanics, a system’s complete state is described by a
wavefunction
, ψ, whose squared magnitude, |ψ|², gives the probability density of finding the particle at a given position. Physical quantities that can be measured (
observables
— position, momentum, energy) are represented by mathematical
operators
acting on the wavefunction. Measuring an observable yields one of the operator’s
eigenvalues
, and after measurement the system collapses into the corresponding
eigenstate
. This is a fundamentally different picture from classical mechanics, where a particle simply has a definite position and momentum at all times.
The
time-dependent Schrödinger equation
, iℏ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ, governs how a quantum state evolves over time, where Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator (representing total energy). For systems with a time-independent potential, this separates into the
time-independent Schrödinger equation

, Ĥψ = Eψ, an eigenvalue equation whose solutions give the allowed (quantized) energy levels of the system — this single equation is the source of quantization in every application: atoms, molecules, and solids.
Quantum angular momentum is quantized — it can only take specific discrete values, unlike the continuous range allowed classically.
Spin

is an intrinsic form of angular momentum with no classical analogue (it is not literally the particle “spinning”); electrons have spin-1/2, meaning their spin angular momentum along any measured axis can only be +ℏ/2 or −ℏ/2. In a magnetic field, this two-valued spin gives rise to two distinct energy levels (splitting observed as the Zeeman effect, discussed below) and is the basis of technologies like MRI and electron spin resonance.

blocks.text: 5. Particle in a box, tunnelling, and the harmonic oscillator

segments.text: The
particle in a box

(a particle confined to a region with infinitely high walls) is the simplest problem showing how boundary conditions on the wavefunction force energy to be quantized — only wavelengths that “fit” the box (analogous to standing waves on a string) are allowed, giving discrete energy levels rather than a continuum.
Quantum tunnelling

is the phenomenon where a particle has a nonzero probability of passing through a potential energy barrier even when its energy is less than the barrier height — classically impossible, but a direct consequence of the wavefunction extending (with exponentially decaying amplitude) into and through the barrier. Tunnelling explains alpha decay in nuclear physics and is the operating principle of the scanning tunnelling microscope.
The
quantum harmonic oscillator

models any system near a stable equilibrium (such as vibrating atoms in a molecule or solid) and has evenly spaced energy levels, E_n = (n + ½)ℏω — notably, even the lowest (“ground”) state has nonzero energy (
zero-point energy
), because the uncertainty principle forbids a particle from having both exactly zero position spread and zero momentum spread.
Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle

, ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2, states that position and momentum cannot both be known to arbitrary precision simultaneously — this is not a limitation of measurement technology but a fundamental property of nature arising from the wave-like description of matter. Mathematically, this arises because position and momentum operators do not
commute
([x̂,p̂] ≠ 0); pairs of observables whose operators fail to commute are subject to an uncertainty relation, while commuting observables can be measured simultaneously with unlimited precision.

blocks.text: 7. The Bohr model, quantum numbers, and the Pauli exclusion principle

segments.text: Bohr’s model of the hydrogen atom (a precursor to full quantum mechanics) proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus only in specific allowed orbits with quantized angular momentum, jumping between orbits by absorbing or emitting a photon of energy equal to the difference between orbit energies — correctly predicting the hydrogen spectrum, though it fails for multi-electron atoms.
Full quantum mechanics describes each electron in an atom by four
quantum numbers
: principal (n, energy level/shell), azimuthal (l, orbital shape/subshell), magnetic (mₗ, orbital orientation), and spin (mₛ). The
Pauli exclusion principle

states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers — this is why electrons fill successive shells and subshells rather than collapsing into the lowest energy state, directly explaining the structure of the periodic table (a link exploited further in Chemistry, Chapter 1).

blocks.text: 8. Atomic spectra and key quantum effects

items.text: discrete emission and absorption lines, corresponding to electrons jumping between quantized energy levels — each element has a unique spectral “fingerprint.”

light striking a metal surface ejects electrons only above a threshold frequency, regardless of intensity, and the ejected electrons’ kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity — explicable only if light delivers energy in discrete quanta (photons), E = hf, as Einstein proposed (for which he won the Nobel Prize).

X-rays scattered off electrons shift to longer wavelength, exactly as expected if the X-ray photon behaves as a particle colliding elastically with the electron, transferring some momentum and energy — further confirmation of light’s particle nature.

a high-energy photon, near a nucleus, can convert entirely into an electron–positron pair (mass created from energy, per E = mc²), provided the photon’s energy exceeds the combined rest-mass energy of the pair.
a correction factor describing how an atomic energy level splits in a magnetic field, accounting for the combined (and differently weighted) contributions of orbital and spin angular momentum.
splitting of atomic spectral lines in an external magnetic field, due to the magnetic-field-dependent energy of different orientations of orbital/spin angular momentum.

inelastic scattering of light by molecules, where the scattered light’s frequency shifts by an amount corresponding to the molecule’s vibrational or rotational energy levels — a key tool for probing molecular structure.
Wave–particle duality (confirmed for both light and matter) means quantum objects require a probabilistic wavefunction description, not a definite classical trajectory.
The Schrödinger equation is the master equation of quantum mechanics; its eigenvalue solutions give the allowed, quantized energies of any bound system.

Quantization of angular momentum, discrete energy levels (particle in a box, harmonic oscillator), and the possibility of tunnelling through classically forbidden regions are all direct consequences of the wave nature of matter.
The uncertainty principle is fundamental, not technological, and follows from the non-commutation of certain operator pairs.

The Pauli exclusion principle, applied to four quantum numbers, explains atomic shell structure and, ultimately, the periodic table; the photoelectric, Compton, and pair-production effects together establish the particle nature of light.
